**seamark 3.0.0: change control over what your coding agents can do.**

First release of the current product. seamark reads the configuration Claude
Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI, VS Code and `devcontainer.json` load,
resolves across scopes and vendors what it actually permits, and says what
changed between two moments.

**Install:** `pip install "git+https://github.com/marcosmatalab/seamark@v3.0.0"`, from the tag;
nothing is published to a package index. One runtime dependency (`cryptography`).
Works offline, with no account and no telemetry.

**The seven commands:** `check`, `diff`, `seal`, `verify`, `keygen`, `scan`,
`watch`.

**What it brings:**

- `check` resolves this repository's surface against 32 documented rules, citing
  for each capability the file it comes from and the vendor merge rule that
  resolved it.
- `diff` compares two git refs or two directories without checking either one
  out, so a `post-checkout` hook in the examined repository never runs.
- `seal` and `verify` sign and verify, offline, a baseline that carries no
  paths, no commands, no URLs and no server names inside it.
- A GitHub Action and a pre-commit hook, both in this repository.
- SARIF 2.1.0 output and a self-contained HTML report.

**If you read the JSON documents:** every contract's `$id` is now under
`github.com/marcosmatalab/seamark/schemas/`, and no longer under a domain named
after the product, which this project does not own and never did - an
identifier that anybody could register is one anybody could answer for. Switch
on `schema_version`, which is in the document and is what these promises are
made about; `docs/CONTRACTS.md` says why an identifier is tied to something
held rather than to something rented.

**What it does not do, said here rather than left for you to work out:** it does
not score anything, it does not judge, it does not infer what it did not
observe, and it does not act on what it sees. Configuration declares; it does
not demonstrate behaviour, and a hook that is written is not a hook that ran.
What could not be resolved comes out INDETERMINATE, is counted separately, and
is never spread across the answers that could be given. The published limits are
in `docs/LIMITS.md`.

**Status:** Beta. 2,708 tests, 90% coverage, green on Python 3.11, 3.12 and
3.13.

**Verifying this release, without trusting the person who cut it.** The wheel
and the sdist were built by `.github/workflows/release.yml` on a GitHub runner,
not on a laptop, and each carries a signed statement of the commit and the
workflow it was built from:

```bash
gh release download v3.0.0 --dir . --repo marcosmatalab/seamark
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
gh attestation verify seamark-3.0.0-py3-none-any.whl --repo marcosmatalab/seamark
gh attestation verify seamark-3.0.0.tar.gz --repo marcosmatalab/seamark
git tag -v v3.0.0
```

`SHA256SUMS` says the files are the ones that were published; the attestation
says where those bytes came from; the tag signature says who cut the release.
The first is a checksum and proves nothing on its own - it is the third line
that makes the first one worth running.

**Coming from 2.x, and the name.** 3.0.0 is not an evolution of the model
scanner, it is another product; if the scanner is what you wanted, it is at
`v2.3.0`, where it is still called what it was called. This repository was
**Actaira** until this release. That name belongs to a different product by the
same author - the AI Act platform - and two unrelated things under one name is
a confusion nobody outside can resolve, so the one that had not been published
under its name yet is the one that moved. The distribution, the command and the
import path are all `seamark`; the repository is
`github.com/marcosmatalab/seamark`; `CHANGELOG.md` draws the line between what
was renamed and what could not be.

**Why 3.0.0 and not 1.0.0.** The repository is the same object, with the same
history and the same tags, and 1.0.0 is already in its changelog. Restarting
would put a second 1.0.0 in one record to spare a stranger the surprise of
meeting a project at 3.0.0 - and that surprise is the honest one, because the
rename is a breaking change for anybody who installed the last release, which
is what a major version is for.
